doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Police stop in Mississippi and other harassment
summary: Brown tells how police stopped her, Charles Brown and Paul Williams near Gulfport, forcing a roadside concert, and mentions a car fire and night court.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You could touch them. They were reachable. They were reachable. Most times we toured in buses, station wagons. And they when you got so-called to the top of the ladder which eventually happened in my case, there were those stars who did have the Cadillacs and whatnot, but you took it on your own, you chanced it, to go to the deep south with that kind of a vehicle. And I got arrested a couple of times. They locked the car up a couple of times, and they want to know how you could afford that even though — I had an experience and when my book comes out it will speak of an occasion in which we were going to Gulfport, Mississippi — Charles Brown, and Paul “Hucklebuck” Williams and myself. And the police stopped us and said that we were doing like 30 miles per hour in a 25 mile zone, something like that. And made us all get out of our cars and of course these were all nice cars, a couple of Chryslers and things remind me right. Anyway what we eventually had to do was when we pulled out all the instruments, to prove that they weren’t stolen, we had to do a concert on the side of the road which was probably the most embarrassing thing that’s ever happened to me. I saw that in a movie recently—

Yes. I don’t know if it happened to them but it happened to me. It did. And I was the only one standing there not doing anything. And my pianist named Lee Anderson, who now is still alive in Seattle. I saw him a couple of years ago and we remembered that all of the musicians had taken out their instruments and were playing, you know, on the side of the road. And this tall policeman says to Lee Anderson, “Well what are you playing?” And he said, “I play piano.” And he said, “Well why are you not playing?” No piano, you know? And in those days, we weren’t carrying electric pianos like they do now, they carry the keyboards and whatnot, you know. And so the officer said, “Well you got five seconds to start playing something.”

The funniest thing happened. Intuitiveness. When it’s about survival you think of something. I’ll never forget the band was playing and he leaned over the hood of the car and started playing on the hood of the car. And the police officers accepted that. He proved that he knew how to move his hands at least. And then last but not least, they looked at me and I would be standing there very arrogant in those days. I didn’t fear death, you understand? And they said, “And who are you?” And I was very vain and I said, “I’m the person who pays all of these musicians” you know. I ended up singing on the side of the road. You know, he brandished his pistol and put his hand on it, and said, “Well let me hear you sing something.” And so there we were, all seven of us, standing on the side of the road as the cars were going by and going around or slowing down, doing this performance. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
You know there’s a classic case of the police harassing Miles Davis ‘cause he had his beautiful Ferrari, and he finally got this license plate that says “I own it.”

I own it, yes. Well those things occurred quite often. I had fire set to my car in Birmingham, you know. We’ve had occasions to be stopped and taken to what we call “night court” where the judge lived back in the woods somewhere, you didn’t go to the station you went to his house. And they tell you that you owed two hundred, three hundred dollars, and they wanted it right then and we had to pay it and all this, to move, you know. Those are some of the reasons that caused me to be a little vain and arrogant and adamant about this music surviving because the people who performed it paid a price for it, you know.
